8. Production architecture: managed first, replaceable later

The most important architectural decision is to keep your SaaS product independent of any one voice provider. That way, you can start with a managed agent API and later move selected customers to a custom real-time pipeline without rewriting the entire product.

React + TypeScript SaaS dashboard

Organizations · Agents · Contacts · Campaigns · Billing

Node.js application API

Auth · Tenant permissions · Consent · Usage ledger · Admin

Call orchestration service

Queue · Concurrency limits · Provider adapter · Webhooks · Retry policy

Managed path

Managed voice-agent API

MVP

Custom path

Telephony + streaming + STT/LLM/TTS

Later

Shared data and operations

PostgreSQL · Object storage · Redis jobs · Metrics · Audit logs

Recommended repository structure

voice-saas/
├── apps/
│   ├── web/                  # React + Vite dashboard
│   └── api/                  # Node.js + Express
├── services/
│   ├── call-orchestrator/    # Campaigns and call lifecycle
│   └── voice-gateway/        # Custom audio streaming, later
├── packages/
│   ├── database/             # Schema and migrations
│   ├── provider-adapters/     # Voice and telephony interfaces
│   ├── billing/              # Usage ledger and pricing
│   └── shared/               # Types and validation
├── infra/
│   └── docker-compose.yml    # Local development
├── tests/
└── docs/

Keep the initial deployment as a modular monolith: one API application with well-separated modules, plus a separate worker only when needed. Do not introduce Kubernetes or a large microservice architecture for a zero-budget prototype.

Provider adapter contract

Define your own interface rather than scattering provider-specific API calls throughout the code.

interface VoiceProvider {
  createAgent(config: AgentConfig): Promise<AgentRef>;
  startCall(input: StartCallInput): Promise<CallRef>;
  endCall(callId: string): Promise<void>;
  verifyWebhook(
    headers: Record<string, string>,
    rawBody: Buffer
  ): Promise<boolean>;
}

This is an illustrative starting point, not a complete production implementation. Each adapter must also normalize provider events, errors, supported languages, recording permissions, and usage reports. A managed provider may not expose all of these operations in exactly this form.

9. Database design for a multi-business SaaS

Use PostgreSQL from the beginning. Every customer-owned record should belong to an organization, even when you’re testing with only one account.

Table	Purpose
users	Login identity and account status
organizations	Each business using the platform
organization_members	User roles and permissions
voice_agents	Agent instructions, language, version and provider
contacts	Customer details and consent metadata
campaigns	Scheduling, limits, and campaign status
campaign_contacts	Each recipient’s campaign state
calls	Provider ID, duration, status, outcome and costs
call_events	Normalized call lifecycle events
transcripts	Conversation text and timestamps
consent_records	Source, purpose, timestamp and evidence
suppression_list	Opt-outs and do-not-contact restrictions
usage_ledger	Immutable usage and credit transactions
webhook_deliveries	Delivery attempts and retry state
audit_logs	Security-sensitive administrative actions

Important design decisions:

* Every tenant-owned table includes organization_id.
* Use PostgreSQL row-level security as an additional isolation layer.
* Use database transactions for credit reservations and deductions.
* Add unique constraints to prevent duplicate provider events and duplicate campaign jobs.
* Store large audio recordings in private object storage, not directly in database rows.
* Use migrations and version-controlled schema changes.

How usage billing should work

Never calculate a customer’s final charge solely from the duration displayed in the browser.

* Reserve a conservative estimated amount before starting an authorized call.
* Receive and verify the provider’s completion event.
* Reconcile billable duration with provider usage records.
* Write a unique usage-ledger transaction.
* Release unused reserved credit or charge the remaining amount.
* Stop future calls if the account reaches its spending limit.

Use idempotency keys and database transactions to prevent duplicate charges when a webhook is delivered more than once. Do not assume a call is free just because the provider reports an error; reconcile the actual usage.

10. Development roadmap

This is a realistic solo-developer sequence for someone building on a ₹0 prototype budget. The schedule is an estimate, not a promise that provider onboarding or production approval will finish within these periods.

Week 1 — Foundation

Free local development

* Set up the monorepo, React dashboard and Express API.
* Add authentication, organizations and role-based access.
* Start PostgreSQL locally with Docker.
* Create database migrations and automated tests. Deliverable: a functioning multi-tenant dashboard with mock data.

Week 2 — Agent builder

* Create, edit, version and preview AI agents.
* Configure Telugu, English and mixed-language behavior.
* Add an FAQ knowledge source and conversation goals.
* Build a simulated conversation mode. Deliverable: an agent can be configured and tested without a phone call.

Weeks 3–4 — Voice proof of concept

* Create a provider adapter and managed-provider integration.
* Test speech recognition and generated Telugu/English speech.
* Configure an approved telephony connection when available.
* Test call setup, interruptions, hang-up, failures and webhook validation. Deliverable: a working end-to-end call to a consenting test participant, if provider access is available.

Weeks 5–6 — Campaign engine

* Add CSV import and validation.
* Implement queue processing, scheduling and per-tenant limits.
* Add consent checks, suppression lists and opt-outs.
* Implement retries, deduplication and campaign pause controls. Deliverable: a controlled test campaign with a small, consented recipient list.

Weeks 7–8 — Billing and hardening

* Build the usage ledger, pricing rules and admin controls.
* Add audit logs, rate limits, secrets management and backups.
* Test cross-tenant access, duplicate webhooks and failure recovery.
* Review data-protection and telecom compliance with qualified advisers and providers. Deliverable: a pilot-ready build, subject to production approvals and live telecom validation.

You can complete the UI, schema, simulated calls, campaign logic and most tests before spending money. Real phone calls, production telephony numbers and managed voice-agent APIs generally require paid service access.

11. ₹0 prototype budget: what is and isn’t possible

Frontend development

React + Vite, local browser

₹0

Backend and job simulation

Node.js, mock providers, local tests

₹0

Database

Local PostgreSQL in Docker

₹0

Voice and telecom integration

Requires provider access; free allowances are not guaranteed

Variable

Production hosting and domain

Can be deferred during local development

Deferred

Provider cost assumptions

Sarvam’s published managed voice-agent pricing currently lists ₹3.50 per conversation minute on pay-as-you-go, excluding GST. Telephony is billed separately. Its documentation lists a ₹0 monthly fee for the pay-as-you-go plan, but prepaid credits are required to use paid services.

The estimates below assume ₹3.50 per agent conversation minute and exclude all telecom charges, taxes, hosting and other expenses.

Monthly agent minutes	AI cost
0	₹0
100	₹350
500	₹1,750
1,000	₹3,500
10,000	₹35,000

The zero-minute case is a local prototype, not a working telephone service.

For a more custom architecture, the separate components would include speech-to-text, language-model inference, text-to-speech and telephony. Costs then depend on the models, audio duration, provider rates and concurrency. A hybrid architecture does not automatically reduce costs; measure the actual cost per successful conversation before choosing which components to replace.

My recommendation: start with a simulated provider and local database. Implement the provider interface and complete the dashboard before committing to any paid voice service. Then validate one real call and measure its total cost before adding campaigns.

12. Security architecture

Because your platform will serve multiple businesses and process customer conversations, tenant isolation and billing integrity are production-critical.

Tenant isolation

Verify the authenticated user’s organization on every request. Never trust a client-supplied organization_id. Enforce authorization in the service layer and use PostgreSQL row-level security as defense in depth.

Credentials and secrets

Keep API keys in server-side environment variables or a secrets manager. Never send provider credentials to React, commit .env files, or log authorization headers. Rotate credentials if exposed.

Webhook verification

Validate provider signatures or documented authentication mechanisms against the raw request body where required. Reject invalid events, deduplicate valid events, and protect endpoints against replay attacks.

Call and recording privacy

Use HTTPS/WSS, private storage, short-lived download links, access controls, retention policies and encryption. Avoid collecting sensitive details that the agent does not need.

Financial safety

Keep an immutable credit ledger, enforce spend caps and reserve funds transactionally. A tenant must never be able to change its own balance or bypass campaign limits.

Abuse prevention and observability

Apply per-tenant call quotas, phone-number validation, account verification, concurrency limits, anomaly detection, and an emergency global kill switch. Monitor latency, failure rates and spending.

Security tests required before a pilot

* Business A cannot view or change Business B’s agents, calls, contacts or credits.
* Forged and replayed provider events cannot produce duplicate charges.
* Concurrent requests cannot overspend an account’s balance.
* A paused campaign cannot continue dispatching queued calls.
* Opted-out contacts are blocked even if they appear in an older CSV.
* Provider outages cannot trigger unlimited retries.
* Recording URLs and transcripts are inaccessible to unauthorized users.
* An administrator can stop all outgoing calls immediately.

13. Indian telecom and data-protection compliance

This is a release gate, not merely a checklist for later.

Telecom rules

On September 18, 2026, TRAI published the Third Amendment to the Telecom Commercial Communications Customer Preference Regulations, 2018. The announced amendments specifically address application-initiated calls, including automated and artificial-voice calls, and require prior declaration of such use to the telecom service provider, including the calling-line identities involved. Undeclared A2P calling is treated as unsolicited commercial communication under the announced framework.

Before activating customer campaigns:

* Determine the applicable classification for each use case: promotional, service, transactional or another permitted category.
* Work with your licensed telecom provider to obtain approved calling resources and complete applicable declarations and registrations.
* Implement consent and DND checks according to the applicable rules and provider requirements.
* Restrict campaign timing, retry policies and dialing rates to the applicable limits.
* Preserve evidence of consent, call purpose, opt-outs and relevant campaign configuration.
* Verify the current regulations, commencement provisions and provider requirements with qualified telecom counsel before launch.

Do not assume that a normal mobile number or a generic cloud telephony API automatically authorizes automated commercial calling.

Official references:

* TRAI — Third Amendment Regulations, 2026⁠￼
* TRAI — Advice to senders⁠￼

Digital Personal Data Protection

The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and DPDP Rules, 2025 establish a framework for lawful processing, transparency, purpose limitation, security and individuals’ rights. The government has also described a phased compliance timeline, so determine which provisions apply to your launch date and role.

For your SaaS product:

* Clearly disclose how phone numbers, transcripts, recordings and summaries will be used.
* Establish the respective responsibilities of your platform and business customers.
* Obtain and document the required permissions and lawful basis for processing.
* Provide appropriate mechanisms for access, correction, erasure and withdrawal of consent where applicable.
* Define retention periods and delete data when retention is no longer justified.
* Document subprocessors, security safeguards, breach response and contractual responsibilities.
* Confirm recording disclosures and consent requirements for each deployment.

A disclaimer alone does not make a calling campaign compliant. Your product should technically prevent campaigns that lack the required authorization.

14. Production-readiness criteria

Before you invite paying customers, require evidence for each of these:

Area	Minimum acceptance criterion
Voice quality	Tested Telugu, English and code-switched conversations, including interruptions
Reliability	Correct recovery from timeouts, disconnects and duplicate events
Isolation	Automated cross-tenant authorization tests pass
Billing	Reconciled provider usage and no duplicate ledger transactions
Campaigns	Consent enforcement, opt-outs, quotas and emergency stop tested
Privacy	Access controls, retention and deletion verified
Compliance	Provider approvals, declarations and legal review completed
Operations	Backups, monitoring, incident procedures and rollback documented

* Test call setup, interruptions, hang-up, failures and webhook validation. Deliverable: a working end-to-end call to a consenting test participant, if provider access is available.

Weeks 5–6 — Campaign engine

* Add CSV import and validation.
* Implement queue processing, scheduling and per-tenant limits.
* Add consent checks, suppression lists and opt-outs.
* Implement retries, deduplication and campaign pause controls. Deliverable: a controlled test campaign with a small, consented recipient list.

Weeks 7–8 — Billing and hardening

* Build the usage ledger, pricing rules and admin controls.
* Add audit logs, rate limits, secrets management and backups.
* Test cross-tenant access, duplicate webhooks and failure recovery.
* Review data-protection and telecom compliance with qualified advisers and providers. Deliverable: a pilot-ready build, subject to production approvals and live telecom validation.

You can complete the UI, schema, simulated calls, campaign logic and most tests before spending money. Real phone calls, production telephony numbers and managed voice-agent APIs generally require paid service access.

12. Security architecture

Because your platform will serve multiple businesses and process customer conversations, tenant isolation and billing integrity are production-critical.

Tenant isolation

Verify the authenticated user’s organization on every request. Never trust a client-supplied organization_id. Enforce authorization in the service layer and use PostgreSQL row-level security as defense in depth.

Credentials and secrets

Keep API keys in server-side environment variables or a secrets manager. Never send provider credentials to React, commit .env files, or log authorization headers. Rotate credentials if exposed.

Webhook verification

Validate provider signatures or documented authentication mechanisms against the raw request body where required. Reject invalid events, deduplicate valid events, and protect endpoints against replay attacks.

Call and recording privacy

Use HTTPS/WSS, private storage, short-lived download links, access controls, retention policies and encryption. Avoid collecting sensitive details that the agent does not need.

Financial safety

Keep an immutable credit ledger, enforce spend caps and reserve funds transactionally. A tenant must never be able to change its own balance or bypass campaign limits.

Abuse prevention and observability

Apply per-tenant call quotas, phone-number validation, account verification, concurrency limits, anomaly detection, and an emergency global kill switch. Monitor latency, failure rates and spending.

Security tests required before a pilot

* Business A cannot view or change Business B’s agents, calls, contacts or credits.
* Forged and replayed provider events cannot produce duplicate charges.
* Concurrent requests cannot overspend an account’s balance.
* A paused campaign cannot continue dispatching queued calls.
* Opted-out contacts are blocked even if they appear in an older CSV.
* Provider outages cannot trigger unlimited retries.
* Recording URLs and transcripts are inaccessible to unauthorized users.
* An administrator can stop all outgoing calls immediately.

13. Indian telecom and data-protection compliance

This is a release gate, not merely a checklist for later.

Telecom rules

On September 18, 2026, TRAI published the Third Amendment to the Telecom Commercial Communications Customer Preference Regulations, 2018. The announced amendments specifically address application-initiated calls, including automated and artificial-voice calls, and require prior declaration of such use to the telecom service provider, including the calling-line identities involved. Undeclared A2P calling is treated as unsolicited commercial communication under the announced framework.

Before activating customer campaigns:

* Determine the applicable classification for each use case: promotional, service, transactional or another permitted category.
* Work with your licensed telecom provider to obtain approved calling resources and complete applicable declarations and registrations.
* Implement consent and DND checks according to the applicable rules and provider requirements.
* Restrict campaign timing, retry policies and dialing rates to the applicable limits.
* Preserve evidence of consent, call purpose, opt-outs and relevant campaign configuration.
* Verify the current regulations, commencement provisions and provider requirements with qualified telecom counsel before launch.

Do not assume that a normal mobile number or a generic cloud telephony API automatically authorizes automated commercial calling.

Official references:

* TRAI — Third Amendment Regulations, 2026⁠￼
* TRAI — Advice to senders⁠￼

Digital Personal Data Protection

The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and DPDP Rules, 2025 establish a framework for lawful processing, transparency, purpose limitation, security and individuals’ rights. The government has also described a phased compliance timeline, so determine which provisions apply to your launch date and role.

For your SaaS product:

* Clearly disclose how phone numbers, transcripts, recordings and summaries will be used.
* Establish the respective responsibilities of your platform and business customers.
* Obtain and document the required permissions and lawful basis for processing.
* Provide appropriate mechanisms for access, correction, erasure and withdrawal of consent where applicable.
* Define retention periods and delete data when retention is no longer justified.
* Document subprocessors, security safeguards, breach response and contractual responsibilities.
* Confirm recording disclosures and consent requirements for each deployment.

A disclaimer alone does not make a calling campaign compliant. Your product should technically prevent campaigns that lack the required authorization.
